speechtext: Harsh.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR COMMITTEE ON ADJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DIVISIONS
speechtext:
It may be harsh, but I have been listening to the remarks about the law of the jungle and about the unfairness of the government, and I regret having to say this, that opposition members have approached the committee on many occasions with suggestions as to what should be done under particular circumstances, and that their suggestions were often acted upon. One would suppose from what has been said in this debate that the government had gone back to the system which obtained prior to the Liberal government of 1903, when for the first time the present system was introduced. One would think perhaps we had presented a blank cheque of some kind to the opposition for signature, and that we asked them to endorse the boundaries of any given constituency as we presented it to them. Sir, that is not what happened. That is not what happened in the last two redistributions. We had members of all opposition parties on all subcommittees. Their suggestions were received and acted upon in many cases; and I came to the conclusion, sir, that if we did not have the attitude referred to by Professor Norman Ward in this particular instance, we would not have any particular complaint about the result of the last redistribution.
However, I may say with respect to Professor Norman Ward-and I say this with respect-I recall that this gentleman had written rather extensively on this particular subject, and in particular he had said it was desirable that parliament should no longer exercise its prerogative in this regard of establishing special rules, so that this, that or the other province would not have a representation that it was not entitled to on a strictly population basis. For that reason I was somewhat surprised to see in the newspapers during the course of the controversy over a year ago that Professor Norman Ward was almost the first one to spring to the defence of the province of Saskatchewan and allege that it should not have its membership reduced though the population itself so required. Indeed, in the article that has been sent to me I find one sentence which reads thus:
The prairie case for special consideration rested on both logical and political grounds.
Therefore I suggest to you, sir, that we should bear in mind that even the best expert will inevitably react to a defence of interests which he believes should be defended, and

that you then have experts doing what in my opinion in the long run must be done by the House of Commons; and that if you are defending political grounds and grounds of logic, as he says here, this is the high court of parliament, and this is the place in which those things must be done.
It follows therefore that any preliminary work which may be undertaken will have to be determined in this House of Commons, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has indicated. But, sir, it should be borne in mind that when you say that you have only a variation of the present system of redistribution. You do not get a new system; you get only some of the preliminary work done by other persons rather than by the committees of the House of Commons and in the end, as I say, if you adopt that view you do away with all the arguments that have been made here as to the political interference of the government or of a party forming the government.
In other words, as I pointed out when we debated this eighteen months ago, when the United Kingdom government presented to parliament the report of the special commission it was accompanied by a bill which said that notwithstanding the report, they were going to do it in some way different from that which was contained in the report. Naturally that announcement was received with a good deal of interest by the opposition, which made a great point of saying that the government were not satisfied on political grounds, and therefore were resorting to a bill which would give them a greater advantage from the standpoint of redistribution. And, as the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickers-gill) pointed out, the government of that day in the United Kingdom happened to be formed by a party which has the admiration of my hon. friends of the C.C.F.
I do not suppose anyone wants to do the extra work involved in the system we have followed in the past two redistributions. I suppose if the preliminary work could be done by others we would all be better satisfied, and I for one can see that there would be an advantage in it. But, as I pointed out eighteen months ago, and I repeat it tonight, hon. members should bear in mind that this system does not get away from the debates in the house about the wisdom or otherwise of a redistribution bill. You will have the debates here, and you will have the debates inevitably turn upon whether or not there is fairness to one or the other member or to a party in the house.
With that in mind I suggest to hon. members-and in particular those who are going to serve on this committee-that they might

consider whether if that political argument is to develop it would be better to do it by way of a committee of the house in any event, or to reserve their decision until a report has been made and then have that particular debate.
No system can be completely divorced from parliament unless you do it in that way, unless you say when you set up your rules that the report of the commission shall be final and parliament shall not intervene. If you are not prepared to go that far, then remember that you are going to have a debate in the House of Commons on the redistribution bill. That is the weakness in the one system. It may be its strength as well, and I am hopeful that when the committee on privileges and elections is seized with this particular resolution they will work on it and bring in a recommendation covering all possible means of carrying out this work that has been given to parliament as one of the things it must do.
Nevertheless, sir, I would not want this resolution to be carried with the impression left in the house that either in 1947 or in 1952 this parliament exercised its prerogative of passing a redistribution bill by a government party doing so without due consideration of all the interests in the country. In my opinion the committee discharged its obligations, not cf course to the satisfaction of everyone. Seldom do we reach that happy state in anything; but I insist that the last two redistributions were as fair as circumstances could make them; that there are members on the opposition side of this house who will agree with me in that respect, and that we should not leave this motion on the basis that it is a reflection on what has been done. Because in my opinion, sir, nearly all the opposition, or nearly all the criticism of what has been done, has been based on an effort to obtain what one might say in private was better terms for himself from the opposition. Indeed there is really no unfairness in either of the past two redistributions. Therefore, sir, I am prepared to support the amendment moved by the Secretary of State, but in doing so I resist any suggestion that we have been in any respect unfair to opposition members.

speechtext:
If the
memory of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) is as good as I think it is, he probably thinks I am getting up to reproach him on having, shall I say, reorganized me out of existence some years ago, but I am not going to do that at all, Mr. Speaker. My wounds are more or less healed, and in any event I am not going to display them.
Redistribution
I was very interested in the certificate of virtue that he has at some length given to his party. I myself am more satisfied with the admission that we are just human beings, which has been made by my leader. I feel, however, that it is an honour to associate with people who never fall below the highest levels of chivalry.
Incidentally, I think we have all been delighted to see the skilful manner in which the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) has descended from those heights of nonpartisanship where he spent many happy years-we used to see him up there in the gallery-and now seems to have come down to the lower levels with the rest of us, and to be remarkably at home. I can only say that if he makes the same progress in the next two or three years that he has made in the last two or three weeks, we may expect almost anything.
I got up tonight merely to say that it seems to me that we are making progress backward at the moment. When the resolution was moved by the hon. member for Quebec South 1 thought it was a sound resolution, particularly in its timing. I think we will all admit, man to man, that when redistribution comes right on top of an election, when people have the scent of battle in their nostrils, it is just almost too much to expect that even with the virtues such as those the minister has expressed-I am sure that he is full with it, bursting with it-even with all the virtue in the world we are not going to make at the suggestion of our friends just a little turn this way and another little turn that way.
It seems to me that this resolution is worth exploring because I think everyone in this house will admit that we are not proud of the way this thing is done now. It may be quite difficult to find a better way; it may be that when we try to find a better way we will come back to this rough and ready, horsetrading plan, but I think it is worth while to give a fair trial to what is proposed in the resolution moved by the hon. member for Quebec South.
The hon. member is not moving it because he is a simpleton in politics. He knows a great deal about politics. When a man like him comes along and suggests this, it is not like something coming from a babe in arms. This is like something from a graduate who is telling us freshmen how to do it.
Amendment (Mr. Pickersgill) agreed to.
Motion as amended agreed to.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. M. Campbell (The Balllefords) moved:
subtopic: SUGGESTED FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
That, In the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of granting financial assistance to the various provinces for the purpose of providing Canada with an adequate highway system.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this morning I did not think for a minute that my resolution would come up tonight, but about noon I was informed that word was going around that most hon. members did not have their speeches ready on their resolutions and that I might have an opportunity this evening to *discuss mine. Because I believe this is one of the major problems facing the country I do mot want to miss an opportunity to speak on this resolution. Therefore I am going ahead tonight, even though I have hurriedly put my notes together and my speech will not be as good as if I had taken a little more time in preparation.
It is not my intention to endeavour to draw a blueprint of the highway needs of Canada, but I do want to point out the terrific need for more, better and safer roads in this country as well as the need for a network of highways to enable our mobile defence units to move rapidly in all directions in the defence of our country.
When the British North America Act was drawn up, horses provided the main method of transportation. At that time roads were a secondary consideration; therefore the fathers of confederation decreed that roads would be the responsibility of the provincial governments. At that time they could not foresee that 30, 40 or 50 years later our whole method of transportation would have changed completely and that huge sums of money would be required to provide an adequate highway system.
The change that has taken place even in my own lifetime is nothing short of a miracle. I can remember getting on a street car in Montreal that was hauled by two horses. There were barns at intervals along the streets to provide for changes of horses. I remember one day in particular when the team of horses pulling the car up Beaver Hall hill got stuck and had to wait until another team could help them.
Of course that stage in transportation has long been passed. I well remember my first visit to Medicine Hat, Alberta, in 1904, when a friend took me for a drive with his new trotter. When we got away from the town there was no road. There were simply trails the full width of the road allowance. When

a trail got down six or eight inches they merely moved over half the width of a wagon and started a new trail. That road for the whole road allowance of 66 feet was just a combination of trails. Of course the poor horse could not show any speed, and my friend could not demonstrate what his horse could do. We had to come back into town to the streets they had there.
I travelled in the summer of 1905 in a wagon train from Medicine Hat some 275 miles north. There were no roads. Part of the way there was a faint trail to follow, but for the rest of the distance we had to go by the sun. We had to send riders ahead to look for water holes where we could camp at night.
It was several years after we homesteaded before any attempt was made to do anything about roads. The first equipment used was a two-horse scraper which was used merely to fill in holes. Then came the four-horse Fresno which was handled by one man and could do about twice as much work. I think it was in 1914 that our municipality bought its first grader. This required twelve horses to haul, and it was the beginning of road making in our district.
I well remember this because I operated that machine part time for the first few years it was used. I remember one farmer coming out and laying into me because he thought I was spoiling his trail. That trail had been worn down until it was smooth, and he saw this machine coming along and apparently tearing up the road.
About that time the odd car made its appearance. But cars could be used only in dry weather because there were no allweather roads. Of course if there was a well-worn trail they might get by even in rainy weather.
From that time road building progressed slowly. Municipalities and provinces were snowed under with demands for roads. With their limited finances they have been unable to keep up with the increased use of motor vehicles for transportation. The horse has completely disappeared from the picture. This means that farmers who could get to town with horses during wet weather and in the winter now have to depend on their cars or even tractors; and when it snows or rains they are marooned.
Many municipalities in the two provinces I know best-I refer to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan-in an attempt to provide roads that can be more easily freed from snow are building high and narrow roads with very steep, sharp ditches. These can only be classified as deathtraps in wet or icy weather. Numbers of large school

units have been formed across Canada necessitating the use of buses to carry the children to school. Many children will be obliged to miss many school hours because the roads in many places are impassable when it rains or snows.
While eastern Canada can boast of more macadam and cement highways, practically all of those that were built before 1940 and many built even later have long passed their usefulness and have become a menace to the motorist. Nearly all our older highways are too narrow, with no passing lanes, and with far too many sharp turns and blind curves. Speed laws are not being enforced. Mr. Speaker, I know they are not being enforced. A couple of weeks ago I travelled from Windsor to Ottawa. All along the highway there were signs that said, "Speed limit 50 miles an hour". Being a good citizen I set my speed at 50 miles an hour and kept it between 50 and 55, but dozens of cars passed me. That road is quite similar to most of our roads here in eastern Canada. There were cars in a hurry watching for an opportunity, in two heavy lines of traffic, to get around me and get ahead so they could make their 60, 70 or 80 miles an hour. I just want to say here that something will have to be done. The speed laws will have to be enforced sooner or later, because most of our accidents are caused by excessive speed. I do not think we can put enough policemen on our highways in order to keep our traffic down to 50 miles an hour.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUGGESTED FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Order. I am entirely unable to ascertain how a discussion of speed laws is relevant to the motion which the hon. member is moving.

subtopic: SUGGESTED FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am just pointing out the fact that, because of the present-day speed of cars, we must have highways that have at least three lanes so those people who want to go faster than does a man of my age, who does not want to go over 50 miles an hour, can get by without endangering other people who are on the highways with them. If we are going to do nothing about our roads, and if we are going to try to keep people down to 50 miles an hour, there is only one solution. That is to put a governor on every car that goes out of the shops. Then and then only will you be able to control the speed on our highways.
Our provincial governments are spending most of their financial resources on the building of main highways, and are leaving most of the responsibility for market roads to the municipalities whose resources are very limited. Across the line in the United States the federal government in 1916 started a federal roads program "to get the farmer
Highways
out of the mud". Because of that program they have developed a great network of highways, but even the great development in that country has not kept pace with modern motor traffic.
Last year the General Motors Corporation of the United States offered a prize of $25,000 for the best essay on how to plan and pay for better highways. The award was given to Robert Moses, New York City commissioner of parks, who in his essay stated that the highway dilemma is a major concern of every man, woman and child in the country and suggested that whereas the United States spent last year $2,700 million on highways, an expenditure of $5 billion per year should be made during the next ten years if the highway system is to be brought up to date.
In 1951 the United States federal government gave in grants to the state governments for primary roads $247,500,000; for secondary roads, $165 million; for urban roads, $137,500,000, making a total of $550 million in grants to help the states out. Besides that the federal government itself built roads to the value of $2,150 million on interstate systems, defence access roads, forest highways, national parkways, park roads and other special purpose roads.
Until the last two years the federal government of Canada has given no assistance to the building of roads in Canada. There are a great many people and a great many organizations across Canada who believe the time has come for the federal government to do something to assist our province in the matter of an adequate highway system for Canada. A good many resolutions have been passed. I have a few of them here that I want to put on the record.
At the annual meeting of the Saskatchewan associated boards of trade held on May 18, 1951 the following resolution was passed;
Whereas in the year ended March 31, 1949, the federal government collected $100 million in sales taxes, excise tax and customs duty on motor vehicles and automotive supplies; and
Whereas up to the present time and including the current appropriation of $150 million toward the construction of the trans-Canada highway, the total all-time federal aid to Canadian highways has amounted only to $170 million;
Now therefore be it resolved that a substantially greater proportion of federal revenue derived from these sources be devoted to assisting the provinces in construction of a national highway system.
The Canadian Good Roads Association have passed resolutions for several years past advocating federal aid to highways.
